one_liner: Abandoned 2013-2015 SIMD array math library (log, exp, sin, dot, sum); hand-tuned assembly only for pre-2015 x86-64 cores.
what_it_does: Yeppp! is a C library of whole-array operations: elementwise add/subtract/multiply in every operand combination, dot product, sum, sum of squares, polynomial evaluation, and double-precision log, exp, sin, cos and tan on arrays (yepMath_Log_V64f_V64f(x, y, length) and similar), plus CPU identification, cycle counters and timers. It is not a scalar libm replacement: you call it on whole arrays, and it returns a status code (null or misaligned pointers give an error, not a crash). Bindings exist for C++, C#, Java and Fortran, and the Julia package Yeppp.jl wraps the Float64 functions.
how_it_is_fast: The kernels are x86-64 assembly generated by the author's PeachPy Python assembler, with one hand-scheduled version per microarchitecture (Bobcat, K10, Nehalem, Sandy Bridge, Bulldozer, Haswell). Log reduces the input to a mantissa in [sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(2)) and evaluates a degree-20 Horner polynomial with a double-double ln2. The Haswell fast path interleaves 10 AVX2/FMA3 vectors (40 doubles) to hide FMA latency and branches to a slower full path only when a batch holds subnormal, zero, negative or infinite values. At yepLibrary_Init() a dispatcher picks the kernel by matching the CPU model it detected against a hard-coded list of microarchitectures.
when_to_use: Legacy code that already uses its array API and runs on the x86-64 cores it was tuned for (Nehalem to Haswell, AMD K10, Bobcat, Bulldozer to Steamroller), where the assembly kernels actually run
Studying how per-microarchitecture assembly is generated (PeachPy) and how a high-degree Horner polynomial is interleaved across many SIMD registers to hide FMA latency
Projects that need one vendored BSD-3 array-math API callable from C, C#, Java and Fortran, and that accept a scalar fallback on everything else
when_not_to_use: Any x86-64 CPU newer than Haswell (Intel) or Steamroller and Jaguar (AMD): the dispatch table has no entry for Broadwell, Skylake or later Intel models, nor for any Zen, so log, exp, sin, cos and tan fall back to a scalar C loop. Users report it slower than plain Julia: i7-6820HQ Yeppp 0.027 s vs loop 0.015 s (Yeppp.jl #32); Yeppp.log! at 0.66x of Base on Julia 0.6.2 (#37)
ARM, PowerPC, MIPS or 32-bit x86: codegen/math.py registers only x64 assembly for the transcendental functions, so those platforms always run the scalar C fallback
Code that can see NaN or +Inf in its input (see gotchas)

Anything needing maintenance, AVX-512 or SVE, a float32 transcendental API, or a buildable source tree. The official Bitbucket repo and its release binaries are gone, and the GitHub mirror lacks the generated yepCore/yepMath sources and headers

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (ships its own runtime library). Building from the mirror needs Python 2.7 plus a 2013-2015 PeachPy to regenerate yepCore/yepMath (not checked in), trunk NASM, and the Java CLIBuild/EBUILDA build or the late Ninja+Python configure.py
integration.min_toolchain: Prebuilt 1.0.0 binaries were built with GCC 4.8, Clang 3.4, Visual Studio 2010/2012 and ICC 13.1.3. BUILD.md warns that builds with an outdated toolchain can produce binaries that crash on some systems
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux/Windows/macOS get assembly kernels only on the listed pre-2015 microarchitectures. x86, ARMv5/v7, PowerPC64/Blue Gene/Q, Xeon Phi k1om and Android MIPS builds exist, but their transcendental functions run scalar C
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. yepLibrary_Init() must run once before any call because it fills global dispatch pointers that start as NULL. The array kernels keep no other state

gotchas: Correctness bug in the scalar C fallback (yepBuiltin_Log_64f_64f in library/headers/yepBuiltin.h). The final '+inf and NaN' fixup tests x after x has been overwritten by the reduced mantissa (always in [0.707, 1.414)), so it never fires. log(NaN) returns 1025*ln2 + ln(0.75) = 710.188 and log(+Inf) returns about 709.78. This matches Yeppp.jl issue #31 exactly ('Yeppp.log([NaN]) = 710.188', open since 2016). That fallback is the path modern CPUs take

The Sandy Bridge and Haswell AVX log fast paths screen inputs with ordered VCMPLTPD/VCMPGTPD against min_normal/max_normal. Those compares are false for NaN, so NaN appears to stay on the fast path and come out near 710. This is from reading the code, not from running it. The Nehalem path uses an unsigned integer range check and does catch NaN

Dispatch matches exact CPU models: the x64 switch in Dispatch.cpp has no case for Broadwell or SkyLake, even though CpuX86.cpp detects them, and CpuX86.cpp does not know Skylake-S/H (model 0x5E), any later Intel core, AMD Excavator or Zen. All of these get the 'Unknown' list and the naive C++ implementation, with no warning

Pointers must be naturally aligned (8 bytes for double) or calls return YepStatusMisalignedPointer. Calling any function before yepLibrary_Init() calls through a NULL dispatch pointer. Tan has assembly only for AMD Bulldozer (FMA4), so on Intel it is always scalar
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Rarely. SLEEF covers the same vector log/exp/sin with documented ulp bounds, is maintained, and supports AVX-512, NEON and SVE. VDT is header-only and inlines into auto-vectorized loops. herumi/fmath is faster for float32 logf/expf. Pick Yeppp! only for legacy code bound to its array API on Haswell-era or older x86-64.
verified_claims_summary: The only number is a Julia-binding README line, written in 2018 by a Julia maintainer after issue #37 disproved the earlier '7x faster than openlibm' line: Yeppp.log! is '3x faster' than Julia's own Base log on 10^7 random Float64. It comes from a single cold @elapsed run of each (JIT and allocation included) with no CPU, Julia version or flags stated. Independent runs on Skylake-era machines found Yeppp slower (0.66x in #37; 0.027 s vs 0.015 s for a plain loop in #32), which the dispatch table explains: those CPUs never reach the assembly kernels.
status_note: Abandoned since 2015 (mirror's last commit 2015-08-24; Yeppp.jl archived 2020-04-09), and the official Bitbucket repo and binaries are gone. BSD-3 lets you vendor it, but on current CPUs it runs a slow scalar fallback with a NaN/+Inf bug, so treat it as historical reference rather than something to copy.
